title: One token through Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
subtitle: What happens between your last word and the model's next one: 48 layers, each with attention and a mixture of experts

nodes.label: Your text
nodes.desc: The conversation so far. The model only ever predicts one next token at a time.

nodes.label: Tokenizer
nodes.desc: Splits text into tokens (word pieces) and turns each into an id number.

nodes.label: Embedding
nodes.desc: Looks up the token id in a table and returns a vector of 2,560 numbers: the token's starting meaning.

nodes.label: Engram table
nodes.desc: A huge lookup table keyed by the last few tokens (n-grams). Which rows a token needs is known the moment the token is known, so they can be fetched from RAM or SSD ahead of time.
nodes.notes: Same idea as DeepSeek's Engram and Tencent Hy4 flash's 64B Engram parameters. With -lzm on, llama.cpp reads only the rows each token needs, which freed 29 GB of RAM in our runs.

nodes.label: Attention
nodes.desc: Mixes in information from earlier tokens. 12 layers look back at every earlier token (full attention, with a KV cache); 36 use a cheaper running summary (linear attention).
nodes.notes: Stays in llama.cpp's CUDA code. Costs about 11 ms per token for all 48 layers together, plus norms, the shared expert and sampling.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.desc: A small matrix scores all 512 experts for this token. The top 10 win; their scores become mixing weights (softmax over the 10).

nodes.label: 512 experts
nodes.desc: Each expert is a small feed-forward network (2560 -> 640 -> 2560, about 3 MB at 4-bit). Only 10 of 512 run for a token, so a 125B-parameter model reads only a few GB per token.
nodes.notes: This is the part we rewrote in Mojo. In llama.cpp it cost 24.7 of 35.7 ms per token; in Mojo it costs 7-9 ms.

nodes.label: Shared expert
nodes.desc: One extra expert every token uses, gated by its own score. Small and always on the GPU.

nodes.label: Combine
nodes.desc: Adds the 10 expert outputs, each times its weight, plus the shared expert, back onto the token's vector. Then the next layer starts.

nodes.label: LM head
nodes.desc: After layer 48, a final matrix scores every token in the vocabulary. Greedy decoding takes the highest; sampling picks among the likely ones.

nodes.label: Next token
nodes.desc: The chosen token is printed and fed back in as the newest input. Then the whole journey repeats.

flows.name: One token, start to finish
flows.desc: The path every generated token takes. At 42.8 tok/s it takes about 23 ms.

steps.note: Your text is split into tokens; only the newest token needs new work.
The token id becomes a vector of 2,560 numbers.
The last few tokens pick rows from the Engram table, known instantly, so they can be prefetched.
Layer 1 begins: attention mixes in what came earlier in the conversation.
The router scores all 512 experts and keeps the best 10.
Only those 10 experts run. This is 70% of llama.cpp's time per token.
Their outputs are mixed by weight and added back. Repeat for all 48 layers.
After layer 48 the LM head scores every possible next token.
One token is chosen, printed, and fed back in. Then it starts again.

flows.name: Where the time goes
flows.desc: llama.cpp's pinned stack: 35.7 ms per token (28 tok/s). With the Mojo expert layer: about 23 ms (42.8 tok/s).

steps.note: Attention, linear attention, norms, shared expert: about 11 ms per token for 48 layers. Unchanged.
Router and top-10 used to bounce through the CPU in llama.cpp. In Mojo they never leave the GPU.
Routed experts: 24.7 ms per token in llama.cpp, 7-9 ms in Mojo. This is the whole speedup.
The Engram table moved from resident in RAM to read on demand, freeing 29 GB for cold experts.
